title: Apartment Photos and Video That Help Lease Units: What to Shoot and What to Avoid
seoTitle: Apartment Photos and Video That Help Lease Units
seoDescription: What to photograph and film at an apartment community, what Google and listing sites show renters, Google Business Profile specs, and the photo mistakes to avoid.
excerpt: Renters want to see the actual unit, not just the model and the pool. Shoot the real floor plans in daylight, label them honestly and keep your Google profile current.
imageAlt: Bright apartment living room with a beige sectional sofa, wall mounted TV and an open kitchen and dining area behind it under recessed lights
imageIdea: Real, unstaged daylight photo of an apartment living room shot wide from a corner at chest height, showing the path into the kitchen, no people, no logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
The photos that help lease units show the actual unit a renter can rent, shot wide and in daylight, plus the few spaces that answer their biggest questions: the kitchen, the bedroom size, the view, parking and the pet areas. Video works best as a short, steady walkthrough of a real floor plan. Avoid heavy filters, wide angle distortion and model unit photos labeled as if they were every unit.

Most communities I look at have plenty of photos. The problem is that many are of the clubhouse and the pool, and few show what the renter is actually signing for.

What do renters want to see in apartment photos?

Renters want unit level detail. In an Apartments.com survey reported by the National Apartment Association, 77% of renters said they want unit specific photos, 67% want unit specific floor plans and 35% want unit specific 3D tours.

That changes the shot list. A beautiful amenity deck is still worth having, but it does not answer "will my couch fit" or "how much light does the second bedroom get." A model unit is fine as long as it is labeled as a model and the finishes match what is actually available.

What should you shoot for each floor plan?

Shoot every floor plan you market, in the same order every time, so renters can compare plans side by side. The set below covers most of what renters ask a leasing agent on a tour.

  1. Living room from the entry, then from the far corner looking back.
  2. Kitchen, with counters and storage visible and appliances closed.
  3. Each bedroom, from the doorway, so the size reads honestly.
  4. Bathroom and closet, including a walk in closet if the plan has one.
  5. Washer and dryer, or the laundry setup the unit actually has.
  6. The view or patio, at the time of day the light is best, and an honest one if it faces a parking lot.
  7. The floor plan drawing, labeled with the plan name used on your website and listings.

Then add the community shots renters need to decide: parking or garages, the dog park and pet wash, the package room, the gym, the pool and the building entrance. If you have a feature that renters search for, such as covered parking or a pet park, make sure there is a clear photo of it.

What does Google show, and what are its photo rules?

Your Google Business Profile shows your photos and photos from the public, and Google sets basic rules for both. Its guidance says a photo should be in focus, well lit, without significant alterations or excessive use of filters or AI, and should represent reality.

That wording is from Google's Business Profile photo tips, which also suggest adding at least three exterior and three interior photos. Google's photos and videos help page lists the technical specs:

ItemGoogle Business Profile guidance
Photo formatJPG or PNG
Photo file sizeBetween 10 KB and 5 MB
Photo resolution720 by 720 pixels recommended, 250 by 250 minimum
Video lengthUp to 30 seconds
Video file sizeUp to 75 MB
Video resolution720p or higher

The 30 second video limit is a good rule for the profile anyway. One floor plan walkthrough, one amenity clip and one short clip of the neighborhood are more useful than a long brand film. For how your profile shows up in AI answers as well as Maps, see Google Business Profile and AI search.

How should photos be labeled on your website?

Give every image a descriptive file name and alt text that says what is in it, and put photos on the floor plan page they belong to. Google uses that text and the surrounding page to understand an image.

Google's image SEO best practices recommend short, descriptive file names over camera defaults, specific alt text, and note that Google pulls information from the page content around the image, including captions. In practice:

  • File name: two-bedroom-kitchen-quartz-counters.jpg, not IMG_4471.jpg.
  • Alt text: "Two bedroom kitchen with quartz counters and an island", not "kitchen" or a string of keywords.
  • Caption or label: plan name, and "model unit" when it is one.

Alt text is also an accessibility feature. Write it for a person using a screen reader, and the search benefit follows.

What should you avoid?

Avoid anything that makes the unit look different from what a renter will walk into. A tour that does not match the photos costs you the lease and often a review.

  • Heavy edits. Over brightened rooms, replaced skies and AI furniture that is not in the unit. Google's own wording asks for photos that represent reality.
  • Extreme wide angle lenses. A bedroom that looks twice its size sets up a disappointing tour.
  • Stale photos. Old finishes, a pool before the renovation, or seasonal decor from last year.
  • Unlabeled model units. If finishes vary by unit or by renovation tier, say so.
  • Residents without permission. Get written releases for anyone recognizable, and run lifestyle shots past your fair housing training so the people shown do not suggest who the community is for.
  • Text and logos on Business Profile photos. Keep specials and branding in posts and on your website, and keep profile photos as clean pictures of the place.

How often should you update photos?

Review your photo set at least once a quarter and after any renovation, new amenity or change in finishes. Check the photos the public has added to your Business Profile at the same time, since those sit next to yours.

During a lease up, update faster: each newly completed amenity and each new floor plan type should be photographed the week it is ready. Our guide to lease up marketing covers that timeline. Photo freshness and Business Profile media are part of what we review for communities working with our multifamily marketing team.

Questions we hear

What photos should an apartment listing include?

Unit specific photos of each floor plan you market: living room, kitchen, bedrooms, bathroom, closet, laundry and view, plus the floor plan drawing and key amenities like parking and pet areas.

What size should Google Business Profile photos be?

Google lists JPG or PNG files between 10 KB and 5 MB, with 720 by 720 pixels recommended and 250 by 250 as the minimum.

How long can a Google Business Profile video be?

Google lists up to 30 seconds, up to 75 MB, at 720p or higher. A short floor plan walkthrough fits well within that.

Can we use model unit photos?

Yes, if they are labeled as a model and the finishes match what renters can actually lease. Renters say they want unit specific photos, so add those where you can.

Should we edit or enhance apartment photos?

Correct exposure and color, but do not add furniture, replace skies or exaggerate space. Google asks for photos without significant alterations or excessive use of filters or AI.

Shoot every marketed floor plan in the same order, in daylight, including the floor plan drawing.

Give every website photo a descriptive file name and alt text, and label model units as models.
